howItWorks.intro: Enter how many nights you'll spend at private campgrounds versus public parks, plus any nights you plan to camp for free, and this tool splits your trip into three cost tiers instead of treating every night the same. Private parks and public parks sit on very different pricing scales, so lumping them together under one blended nightly rate hides where your money is actually going.

rules.name: Total Cost
rules.explanation: Average rates for private and public campgrounds.

howItWorks.outro: The $55 and $30 figures behind those two tiers are blended national averages — a real full-hookup site at a KOA-style resort during peak season can run well past $55, while an off-season state park pull-through can undercut $30. Swap in your own quoted rates whenever you have them; the built-in averages are meant for early trip planning, not for locking in a final budget.

faq.question: What's the real difference between a full-hookup site and an electric-only site?
faq.answer: Full hookup means 30/50-amp electric, fresh water, and sewer all at your site, so you never have to move the rig to dump or fill. That convenience typically adds $8-15/night over electric-and-water-only, and $15-25/night over a dry (no-hookup) site. If you're only staying one or two nights and your tanks aren't close to full, electric-only or dry camping is usually the better trade — you'll dump on your way out for a few dollars at most private parks.

faq.question: Are state parks and national forests actually cheaper than private RV parks?
faq.answer: Almost always. State park RV sites with electric typically run $20-35/night, and many national forest and BLM dispersed sites are free with a 14-day stay limit. What you give up is amenities — pull-through sites, full hookups, a pool, and a camp store — plus you'll often need a generator or solar setup for dry camping. Private parks like KOA charge $40-70/night but bundle in Wi-Fi, laundry, and sometimes a resort-style layout that's worth it for longer stays with kids or pets.

faq.question: Do camping membership programs like Passport America or Thousand Trails actually pay off?
faq.answer: Passport America gives roughly 50% off at participating private parks (with blackout dates and stay limits at many locations), which can turn a $50/night site into $25 and often pays for its annual fee in three or four stops. Thousand Trails works differently — it's a zone-based membership where nights at its own network of campgrounds are effectively free after the membership fee, which makes the most sense if you camp 30+ nights a year and your route runs through its parks. If you camp fewer than a handful of nights annually or stick to public land, neither program is worth the upfront cost.

faq.question: How much do campground rates change by season?
faq.answer: A lot. Peak-season sites in popular regions (coastal areas in summer, desert parks in winter) can run 20-40% above shoulder-season rates, and some private parks add weekend or holiday surcharges on top of that. Booking a month or two off-peak, or shifting a trip by even a week or two around a holiday weekend, is one of the more reliable ways to cut real dollars off a multi-night stay.

faq.question: How do I decide how many nights to book private versus public for a trip?
faq.answer: Start with what your rig actually needs — if you're running an RV air conditioner or CPAP machine every night, dry camping stretches on batteries alone gets uncomfortable fast, so plan private or electric-hookup nights around those stretches. Then fill the rest of the itinerary with state parks or dispersed sites near the routes you're already driving. Run this calculator with a couple of different splits (say, 70/30 private-to-public versus 40/60) to see how much the mix actually saves before you start booking.

faq.question: Does this calculator include propane, generator fuel, or dump station fees?
faq.answer: No — it estimates site fees only, using blended average rates for private and public campgrounds. Propane, generator gas, extra vehicle or pet fees some parks charge, and one-off dump station fees at free dispersed sites are worth adding on separately since they vary widely by region and rig size.

howWeCalculate.intro: The math is deliberately simple: each night you plan to spend at a private park is priced at a $55 blended average, each night at a public/state park is priced at $30, and free camping nights (dispersed BLM land, national forest boondocking, driveway or Harvest Host stays) contribute nothing to the total. Take an example 14-night trip split into 8 private nights and 6 public nights: 8 × $55 = $440 for the private stretch, 6 × $30 = $180 for the public stretch, for a total of $620 in site fees and an average of about $44.29/night across the whole trip. Book that same 14 nights entirely at private parks and you'd pay 14 × $55 = $770 — the mixed itinerary saves $150, roughly 19% less.
steps: Enter total nights for the trip you're budgeting
Split those nights into private-park nights and public/state-park nights
Enter any free camping nights (dispersed, boondocking, or driveway stays) separately
The calculator applies the $55 private and $30 public averages and totals everything instantly in your browser — nothing is sent to a server
howWeCalculate.disclaimer: These are planning-stage estimates built on blended national averages, not quoted rates. Confirm actual site prices with the campground or booking platform before finalizing a trip budget, since regional pricing, season, and rig size all move the real number.

whenToUse.intro: This tool is most useful in the trip-planning stage, before you've booked a single site, when you're still deciding how many nights to spend at resort-style parks versus public land and want to see the dollar impact of that choice.

sections.title: What the RV Campground Budget Calculator Does
sections.body: This calculator splits an RV trip into three buckets — nights at private campgrounds, nights at public or state parks, and free camping nights — and prices each bucket separately instead of averaging your whole trip into one flat nightly rate. Enter your total nights, how many of those land at private parks versus public parks, and how many are free (dispersed BLM land, national forest boondocking, Harvest Host, a friend's driveway), and it returns your total site-fee cost and the true average cost per night once all three tiers are blended together.

sections.title: Why Campground Rates Swing From $0 to $70+ a Night
sections.body: The gap between camping options comes down to hookups and land ownership. A full-hookup site — 50-amp electric, fresh water, and sewer all at your rig — at a private, KOA-style resort typically runs $40-70/night, more in peak season or coastal/mountain destinations. Drop to electric-and-water-only or electric-only and you'll usually save $10-20/night at the same park. Public options run cheaper across the board: state park sites with electric hookups generally land at $20-35/night, and national forest or BLM dispersed camping is frequently free, though you're managing your own water, power, and waste with no hookups at all. Membership programs change the math further — Passport America typically cuts 50% off participating private-park rates, while Thousand Trails bundles nights at its own campground network into a flat annual or zone fee, which pays off fastest for RVers who camp heavily and stay within its footprint. Rates also move with the calendar: peak-season pricing in popular regions can sit 20-40% above what the same site charges in the shoulder season.

sections.title: When to Run the Numbers
sections.body: Use this calculator while you're still shaping an itinerary — before you've booked sites — to see how shifting nights between private and public campgrounds changes the total. It's also useful for testing whether a membership program is worth buying before a specific trip, and for comparing a faster, more comfortable route (mostly private, full-hookup) against a slower, cheaper one leaning on public land and free camping.

howToSteps.title: Enter Total Nights for the Trip
howToSteps.description: Start with the full length of your trip in nights — this is the number the other three fields need to add up to.

howToSteps.title: Break Nights Into Private and Public Parks
howToSteps.description: Enter how many nights you expect at private campgrounds (full-hookup RV parks and resorts) and how many at public or state parks. These two tiers carry very different average rates, so splitting them out is what makes the estimate useful.

howToSteps.title: Add Free Camping Nights
howToSteps.description: Enter any nights you plan to camp for free — dispersed BLM or national forest boondocking, Harvest Host stops, or staying with friends or family. These nights add zero dollars to the total but still count toward your trip length.

howToSteps.title: Calculate and Review the Breakdown
howToSteps.description: Click Calculate to see your total campground cost and average cost per night. Adjust the private/public split and re-run it to see how much a heavier public-land itinerary would save versus an all-private trip.

tips: Get real quotes for at least your first few stops before finalizing a budget — the $55/$30 averages here are for early planning, not for locking in numbers.
If you'll camp 20+ nights a year and lean on private parks, price out Passport America or Thousand Trails separately — either can cut effective private-night costs by roughly half.
Shift a trip a week or two outside peak season where you can; shoulder-season rates commonly run 20-40% below peak pricing at the same campground.
Weigh hookup level against your actual stay length — paying extra for full sewer hookups rarely pays off on a one- or two-night stop where you won't fill your tanks anyway.
Before counting on free dispersed camping, check the 14-day stay limit typical on BLM and national forest land and confirm current fire or access restrictions for the area.
